title: Plans & the future
goal: Talk about plans, intentions, hopes and dreams using the future tense and 'want to'.
intro: The Odia future is formed with **-ଇବ-** plus the person ending: ମୁଁ ଯିବି 'I'll go', ଆପଣ ଯିବେ 'you'll go'. The 'we' form doubles as **'let's'** (ଚାଲ ଯିବା 'let's go'). You also learn how to say what you *want to* do and what you're *supposed to* do.

phrases.en: What are your plans for next week?
I'll go home for the holidays.
My dream is to travel all over India.
Have you booked the ticket yet?

grammar.title: The future tense: -ଇବି, -ଇବ, -ଇବେ
grammar.body:
Stem + **-ଇବ-** + person ending:
ମୁଁ କରିବି *kôribi* — I will do
ଆମେ କରିବା *kôriba* — we will do; **let's do** (colloquially also କରିବୁ)
ତୁ କରିବୁ *kôribu* — you (intimate) will do
ତୁମେ କରିବ *kôribô* — you (familiar) will do
ଆପଣ କରିବେ *kôribe* — you (formal) will do
ସେ କରିବ *kôribô* — he/she will do
ସେ / ସେମାନେ କରିବେ *kôribe* — he/she (resp.) / they will do

Short stems: ଯିବି, ଆସିବି, ଖାଇବି, ଦେବି, ନେବି, ହେବି. Negative: add ନାହିଁ — ମୁଁ ଯିବି ନାହିଁ. The future is also the polite way to make offers and gentle requests (ଚା ପିଇବେ? / ଏଠି ରଖିବେ?). For plans already fixed, the present continuous works too: ମୁଁ କାଲି ଯାଉଛି.

examples.en: I'll go to Delhi next month.
We'll watch the Chariot Festival. / Let's watch it.

grammar.title: Want to, would like to, supposed to
grammar.body:
**-ବାକୁ ଚାହେଁ** 'want to': ମୁଁ ଯିବାକୁ ଚାହେଁ 'I want to go' (ଆପଣ ଚାହାନ୍ତି, ତୁମେ ଚାହଁ).
**ମୋର -ବାକୁ ଇଚ୍ଛା (ଅଛି)** 'I'd like to' — softer and very common.
**ମୋର -ବା କଥା** 'I'm supposed to / due to': କାଲି ମୋର ଯିବା କଥା 'I'm supposed to go tomorrow'.
**-ବାର ଯୋଜନା କରିବା** 'to plan to'.

The verb in **-ବାକୁ** is the verbal noun in the dative ('to going'), the same form used with ପଡ଼ିବା in Unit 15.

examples.native: ମୁଁ ଓଡ଼ିଆ ଭଲ ଭାବରେ ଶିଖିବାକୁ ଚାହେଁ।
examples.roman: muṃ Oṛia bhôlô bhabôre sikhibaku chaheṃ.
examples.en: I want to learn Odia properly.

examples.native: କାଲି ମୋର ଡାକ୍ତରଙ୍କ ପାଖକୁ ଯିବା କଥା।
examples.roman: kali morô ḍaktôrôṅkô pakhôku jiba kôtha.
examples.en: I'm supposed to go to the doctor tomorrow.

examples.native: ଆମେ ଆସନ୍ତା ବର୍ଷ ନୂଆ ଘର କିଣିବାର ଯୋଜନା କରୁଛୁ।
examples.roman: ame asônta bôrsô nua ghôrô kiṇibarô jojôna kôruchhu.
examples.en: We're planning to buy a new house next year.

dialogue.title: Plans for Rath Yatra
dialogue.setting: Lipi and Sam talk about going to Puri for the Chariot Festival.

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.native: ସାମ୍, ଆସନ୍ତା ମାସରେ ରଥଯାତ୍ରା। ତୁମର କ'ଣ ଯୋଜନା?
lines.roman: Sam, asônta masôre Rôthôjatra. tumôrô kôṇô jojôna?
lines.en: Sam, Rath Yatra is next month. What are your plans?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.native: ମୁଁ ପୁରୀ ଯାଇ ରଥଯାତ୍ରା ଦେଖିବାକୁ ଚାହେଁ।
lines.roman: muṃ Puri jai Rôthôjatra dekhibaku chaheṃ.
lines.en: I want to go to Puri and see the Chariot Festival.

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.native: ବହୁତ ଭିଡ଼ ହେବ, ଜାଣିଛ? ଲକ୍ଷ ଲକ୍ଷ ଲୋକ ଆସିବେ।
lines.roman: bôhutô bhiṛô hebô, jaṇichhô? lôkhyô lôkhyô lokô asibe.
lines.en: It'll be very crowded, you know? Hundreds of thousands of people will come.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.native: ଜାଣେ। ସେଥିପାଇଁ ମୁଁ ଆଗରୁ ହୋଟେଲ ବୁକ୍ କରିବି।
lines.roman: jaṇe. sethipaiṃ muṃ agôru hoṭelô buk kôribi.
lines.en: I know. That's why I'll book a hotel in advance.

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.native: ଆମ ପରିବାର ବି ଯିବ। ଆମ ସହ ଚାଲ।
lines.roman: amô pôribarô bi jibô. amô sôhô chalô.
lines.en: My family is going too. Come with us.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.en: Really? Then it'll be great fun!

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.native: ଆମେ ଆଗଦିନ ସଞ୍ଜରେ ବାହାରିବା, ଆଉ ମାଉସୀ ଘରେ ରହିବା।
lines.roman: ame agôdinô sôñjôre bahariba, au mausi ghôre rôhiba.
lines.en: We'll set off the evening before and stay at my aunt's.

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.native: କିଛି ନାହିଁ। କେବଳ ହାଲୁକା ଲୁଗା ପିନ୍ଧିବ, କାରଣ ବହୁତ ଗରମ ହେବ।
lines.roman: kichhi nahiṃ. kebôḷô haluka luga pindhibô, karôṇô bôhutô gôrômô hebô.
lines.en: Nothing. Just wear light clothes, because it'll be very hot.

culture: During **Rath Yatra**, Jagannath, his brother Balabhadra and sister Subhadra leave the Puri temple on three huge wooden chariots, rebuilt every year, and are pulled by devotees along the Bada Danda (Grand Road) to the Gundicha temple. It is the one time anyone, of any faith, can see the deities. The English word *juggernaut* comes from Jagannath.
